clinical_significance: Subacromial bursitis / rotator cuff impingement syndrome -- by far the most clinically important bursa of the shoulder and a very common ultrasound-guided corticosteroid injection target. Normally does NOT communicate with the glenohumeral joint; if contrast/injectate is seen crossing between bursa and joint, this implies a full-thickness rotator cuff tear.
function: Separates the rotator cuff tendons and humeral head from the overlying coracoacromial arch and deltoid, allowing near-frictionless gliding between them during shoulder elevation; the largest bursa in the shoulder region.
source: as cited in this atlas's uploaded shoulder muscle reference document (shoulder_muscles_reference_v1.html), which draws on Standring S, Tubbs SR (eds), Gray's Anatomy, 43rd ed. (2026), and Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th ed. (2023)

injection_approach.transducer_placement: Use the same longitudinal supraspinatus-tendon view used for cuff assessment: arm in the modified Crass position (hand on the ipsilateral posterior hip pocket) to bring the tendon anterior to the acromion. The bursa is the thin space directly superficial to the tendon and deep to the deltoid; the injection is delivered into this space rather than into the tendon substance.
injection_approach.depth_layer: Immediately deep to the deltoid muscle and superficial to the supraspinatus tendon/greater tuberosity; distinguishing bursal fluid or synovial thickening from the tendon itself is the key identification step before needle advancement.
injection_approach.identification_cues: Anechoic-to-hypoechoic distension, synovial thickening with Doppler flow in bursitis, and gliding of the bursal walls relative to the tendon on passive arm rotation; a normal, non-inflamed bursa is often not separately visible as a distinct fluid stripe.
structures_at_risk: long head of biceps tendon and rotator interval (anterior extension of the bursa)
axillary nerve, if the needle strays inferiorly toward the quadrangular space
injection_approach.notes: This is the single most common ultrasound-guided corticosteroid injection target in the shoulder, for subacromial impingement/rotator-cuff-related bursitis. It is distinct from the deeper cuff-tendon PRP target already documented in this atlas at data/tendons/upper_limb_tendons.json (rotator_cuff_tendon_complex_r/l, prp_injection_approach), whose modified-Crass transducer positioning this bursal approach reuses -- the bursal injection stays superficial to the tendon rather than peppering the tendon substance itself.
injection_approach.source: Transducer positioning cross-referenced from Diaconu S et al., 'A Visual Guide to Ultrasound-Guided Botulinum Toxin Injection in Spasticity: Part II -- Proximal Upper Limb Muscles', Toxins 17(6):276 (2025), doi:10.3390/toxins17060276, and this atlas's own data/tendons/upper_limb_tendons.json rotator_cuff_tendon_complex prp_injection_approach entry; bursal anatomy per this atlas's uploaded shoulder muscle reference document (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, deltoid, subscapularis sections).

clinical_significance: A true anterior joint recess rather than an independently diseased bursa: it normally communicates with the glenohumeral joint (between the superior and middle glenohumeral ligaments) and distends with glenohumeral synovitis or effusion.
function: Lies between the subscapularis tendon and the scapular neck, letting the tendon glide over the anterior glenoid rim/neck during rotation; because it communicates with the joint it functions as an anterior extension of the glenohumeral synovial cavity.
source: as cited in this atlas's uploaded shoulder muscle reference document (shoulder_muscles_reference_v1.html), which draws on Standring S, Tubbs SR (eds), Gray's Anatomy, 43rd ed. (2026), and Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th ed. (2023)

clinical_significance: Relevant to subcoracoid impingement of the subscapularis tendon by a narrowed coracohumeral interval. May communicate with the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa but not with the glenohumeral joint -- a distinction relevant when interpreting bursal distension patterns on imaging.
function: Lies between subscapularis and the coracoid process/conjoint tendon (short head of biceps + coracobrachialis), cushioning the subscapularis tendon against the coracoid during arm motion.
source: as cited in this atlas's uploaded shoulder muscle reference document (shoulder_muscles_reference_v1.html), which draws on Standring S, Tubbs SR (eds), Gray's Anatomy, 43rd ed. (2026), and Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th ed. (2023)

clinical_significance: Small and usually clinically silent, but occasionally communicates with the glenohumeral joint in individual specimens; relevant when a posterior joint injection or aspirate unexpectedly tracks into this plane.
function: Small bursa between the infraspinatus tendon and the postero-lateral joint capsule, reducing friction as the tendon glides during external rotation.
source: as cited in this atlas's uploaded shoulder muscle reference document (shoulder_muscles_reference_v1.html), which draws on Standring S, Tubbs SR (eds), Gray's Anatomy, 43rd ed. (2026), and Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th ed. (2023)

clinical_significance: A classic site of symptomatic scapulothoracic crepitus/bursitis ('snapping scapula'). The spinal accessory nerve runs along its wall approximately 2.7 cm lateral to the superomedial angle -- a described surgical landmark to protect during bursectomy.
function: Gliding-plane bursa between the superomedial scapula and the overlying trapezius, part of the layered soft-tissue system of the scapulothoracic articulation.
source: Williams GR Jr, Shakil M, Klimkiewicz J, Iannotti JP. Anatomy of the scapulothoracic articulation. Clin Orthop Relat Res. 1999;(359):237-246 -- as cited in this atlas's uploaded shoulder muscle reference document (shoulder_muscles_reference_v1.html), which draws on Standring S, Tubbs SR (eds), Gray's Anatomy, 43rd ed. clinical_significance: One of the two consistently-described deep scapulothoracic bursae (with the supraserratus bursa below); a site of symptomatic scapulothoracic crepitus/bursitis when irritated.
function: Gliding-plane bursa between serratus anterior and the chest wall, allowing the scapula (via serratus anterior) to slide over the ribs during protraction, retraction and rotation.
source: Williams GR Jr, Shakil M, Klimkiewicz J, Iannotti JP. Anatomy of the scapulothoracic articulation. name_ta: Bursa intertendinea mm. teretis majoris et latissimi dorsi
clinical_significance: Not independently a major clinical entity in the source document, but relevant to interpreting posterior-axillary-fold imaging and pain, since the two tendons are closely apposed and often partly fused at their insertion.
function: Separates the teres major and latissimus dorsi tendons where they converge near/on the intertubercular groove to form the posterior axillary fold; a further, separate subtendinous bursa may lie between the combined tendon complex and the humerus itself.
source: as cited in this atlas's uploaded shoulder muscle reference document (shoulder_muscles_reference_v1.html), which draws on Standring S, Tubbs SR (eds), Gray's Anatomy, 43rd ed. (2026), and Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th ed. (2023)
